extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (design patent examiners, applicants, and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating design patent applications for novelty (35 U.S.C. 102) and nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), including form paragraphs, evidentiary standards, and how to treat foreign filings, functional/hidden features, analogous art, and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional and hidden features — ornamentality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary for the examiner to cite or apply prior art to show that functional and/or hidden features are old in the art as long as the examiner has properly relied on evidence to support the prima facie lack of ornamentality of these individual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant wishes to rely on functional or hidden features as a basis for patentability, the same standard for establishing ornamentality under 35 U.S.C. 171 must be applied before these features can be given any patentable weight. Examiners must provide evidence to support the prima facie functionality of such features. Hidden portions or functional features cannot be relied upon as a basis for patentability. See MPEP § 1504.01(c). Case citations: Jones v. Progress, In re Cornwall, In re Garbo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception for statutory bars (design patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use exception to a statutory bar for public use or sale does not usually apply for design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, Tone Brothers v. Sysco held that 'experimentation directed to functional features of a product also containing an ornamental design may negate what otherwise would be considered a public use within the meaning of section 102(b).' See MPEP § 2133.03(e)(6). Examiners should apply this limited exception where experimentation relates to functional features but consider ornamentality separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign registration considered equivalent to patenting for 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 35 U.S.C. 102(d), whether or not the foreign grant is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the foreign applicant has received protection in the foreign country, a claim for priority will vest if the U.S. application is timely filed. To avoid statutory bars under 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172, the U.S. design patent application must be filed within six (6) months of the foreign filing. The MPEP includes a table listing country-specific dates which can be used for 102(d) purposes (e.g., date of registration/grant, filing date, publication date) and notes that foreign laws vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 rejections — timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(d) as modified by 35 U.S.C. 172 should only be made when the examiner knows that the application for foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on an application filed more than six (6) months prior to the U.S. filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the grant of a foreign registration/patent is not evident from the U.S. application record or the provided charts, the examiner should include the specified form paragraph (¶ 15.03.01) acknowledging the foreign filing and reminding applicant that a matured foreign protection before the U.S. filing may constitute a statutory bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bracket [1] to identify the reference applied against the claimed design. Include applicable Examiner Notes where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, or in public use or on sale in this country more than one (1) year prior to the application for patent in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert the reference in bracket [1] and explain basis (publication date, public use, or on sale) supporting the one-year statutory bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(c) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) because the invention has been abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when abandonment is the basis for rejection; include supporting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(d), as modified by 35 U.S.C. 172, as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was first patented or caused to be patented, or was the subject of an inventor’s certificate by the applicant, or his/her legal representatives or assigns in a foreign country prior to the date of the application for patent in this country on an application for patent or inventor’s certificate filed more than six (6) months before the filing of the application in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert the foreign reference in bracket [1]. Ensure the timing and issuance facts meet the >6 month and prior-grant requirements before making this rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being clearly anticipated by [1] because the invention was described in a patented or published application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert reference in bracket [1]. For determining the 102(e) effective date, follow American Inventor's Protection Act rules and the Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12/7.12.01 when appropriate (consider international application dates and continuations).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when derivation or inventorship issues indicate the applicant is not the original inventor; include supporting facts and references to required statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) rejection (form paragraph ¶ 15.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) because, before the applicant's invention thereof, the invention was made in this country by another who had not abandoned, suppressed or concealed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when another party in the U.S. made the invention earlier and did not abandon/suppress/conceal. Include necessary facts to support the priority finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical claim: common assignee (¶ 15.24.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is directed to the same invention as that of the claim of commonly assigned copending application No. [1]. The issue of priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly 35 U.S.C. 102(f) of this single invention must be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the USPTO normally will not institute an interference between commonly owned applications or a patent and an application, the assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation. Failure to comply will result in abandonment of this application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a),(b),(d),(e) (¶ 15.15.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape and appearance of [1] is identical in all material respects to that of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph should be included after the applicable 102 rejection to explain the basis of the rejection; insert the claimed design reference in bracket [1] and identify the claimed design. Explain how material identity in shape and appearance supports anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design disclosed but not claimed in another application with common inventor/assignee (¶ 15.15.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. This is a provisional rejection based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested ways to overcome: (A) show derivation under 37 CFR 1.132; (B) show a date of invention prior to the reference under 37 CFR 1.131; (C) perfect priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority documents meeting 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph requirements; or (D) perfect priority under 35 U.S.C. 120 by amending spec or filing ADS under 37 CFR 1.76/1.78(a) and establishing enablement/description per 35 U.S.C.112. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Include bracket insertions for application and inventor/assignee as noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design claimed in earlier-filed design patent application with common inventor/assignee (¶ 15.15.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by the claim in copending Design Patent Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome by abandoning the earlier-filed copending application. Use bracket [2] to insert inventor or assignee. Precede with paragraph 15.24.05 to notify applicant of priority issues under 102(f)/(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design disclosed but not claimed in a patent (¶ 15.15.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested ways to overcome are similar to provisional copending-application rejections: derivation showing, proof of earlier invention, perfecting priority under 119 or 120 with certified documents, and meeting 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements. This rejection may not be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Use brackets to insert patent number(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection maintained (¶ 15.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments presented have been carefully considered, but are not persuasive that the rejection of the claim under [1] should be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form paragraph in subsequent actions where the original rejection is maintained. Insert the statutory basis in bracket [1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness requirement for designs (35 U.S.C. 103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design that meets the test of novelty must additionally be evaluated for nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between claimed and prior art; level of ordinary skill; objective evidence/secondary considerations). Consider design-specific precedents and the overall appearance test for design patent obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries applied to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic factual inquiries guiding evaluation of obviousness are: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluating objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these inquiries as the framework for assessing prima facie obviousness of design claims, supplemented by design-specific case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the prior art — analogous arts for design
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of relevant prior art for evaluating obviousness extends to all 'analogous arts.' The question in design cases is whether the references are so related that the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest the application of those features to the other (In re Glavas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is merely applying attractive appearance to a surface, the nature of the article (wallpaper, oven door, crockery) is immaterial. However, where combining involves material modifications of basic form, the nature of the articles is a definite factor. Use this design-focused guidance to supplement general analogous art requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — overall appearance test
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered. The mere fact that there are differences between a design and the prior art is not alone sufficient to justify patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All differences between the claimed design and the closest prior art reference should be identified in any rejection under 103(a). If differences are de minimis or inconsequential from a design viewpoint, the rejection should state so. Case citations: In re Leslie, In re Lamb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art — designer perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be evaluated from the perspective of a 'designer of... articles of the types presented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the designer-of-the-article standard (In re Nalbandian, In re Carter) when assessing whether a claimed design would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations such as commercial success and copying of the design by others are relevant to evaluating obviousness of a design claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider any objective evidence presented by applicant (including affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132). For commercial success, evaluate whether there is objective evidence and whether the success can be attributed to the ornamental design (nexus required). Expert testimony must establish credentials and should not express an opinion on the ultimate legal issue of obviousness. Copying requires more than mere copying to be significant (consider market factors). See Litton System v. Whirlpool, Avia Group v. L.A. Gear, Panduit, Cable Electric Products v. Genmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness standard for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish prima facie obviousness, all the claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art. The proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary reference must be more than a design concept; it must have an appearance substantially the same as the claimed design. Absent such a reference, no holding of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) can be made, whether based on a single reference or in view of secondary prior art. Avoid basing obviousness on selecting/combining features to create something that did not exist as a 'something in existence' (In re Jennings, In re Rosen, In re Harvey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art references — suggestion/motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) is appropriate if a designer of ordinary skill would have been motivated to modify a primary reference by deleting features thereof or by interchanging with or adding features from pertinent secondary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary references must provide some suggestion to modify the basic design (In re Borden). The longstanding test: whether the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest application of those features to the other (In re Glavas). If secondary references are used to show differences are minor, they should be applied so as to leave no doubt those differences would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill (In re Sapp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on destroying broad function when combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed combination of references so alters the primary reference that its broad function can no longer be carried out, the combination would not have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to modify the primary reference to the extent the specific function may be affected while the broad function is not affected. Example: modifying a cabinet so it is no longer airtight is permissible if the broad function as a cabinet is not impaired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for configuration changes vs surface ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a modification to a primary reference involves a change in configuration, both the primary and secondary references must be from analogous arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, when modifying the surface of a primary reference to provide an attractive appearance, it is immaterial whether the secondary reference is analogous art, since such a modification does not change configuration or destroy characteristics of the primary reference (In re Glavas). Also, simulative design portions may broaden what is considered analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal of prima facie case — applicant evidence and examiner evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness has been established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut it with objective evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rebuttal evidence submitted by applicant, including 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations, must be considered. For commercial success evidence, examiners must determine whether there is objective evidence and whether there is a nexus to the ornamental design. Expert testimony must show credentials and avoid legal conclusions. Copying evidence needs more than mere copying to be significant. A reference may 'teach away' if it would lead a person of ordinary skill in a divergent direction (In re Haruna). See MPEP § 716–716.06 for additional info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Use provided form paragraphs to state 103(a) rejections and prefatory/rationale language (¶ 15.18, ¶ 15.70, ¶ 15.67, ¶ 15.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶ 15.18: single-reference 103(a) rejection wording; ¶ 15.19: multiple-reference 103(a) rejection wording ('The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [1] in view of [2]'). ¶ 15.70 preface: 'It would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to [1].' ¶ 15.67 provides rationale about unobviousness in overall appearance (not minute details). Insert explanations and supporting facts into the brackets as directed.
